noteBlocks.lede: Some metals fizz the moment they touch water; others sit in a drawer for years and never change. The difference is how readily a metal gives its outer electrons away, and putting the metals in that order lets you predict every reaction in this topic instead of guessing.

noteBlocks.text: The reactivity series: air, water and steam

noteBlocks.md: Drop a lump of calcium into water and it fizzes straight away. A copper coin can sit in a puddle for years and stay a coin. Metals differ in how readily they react, and chemists line them up in one fixed order — the reactivity series — so the differences can be predicted instead of guessed.

noteBlocks.text: 1. Reactivity means letting go of electrons

noteBlocks.alt: A magnesium atom drawn with two electrons in its dashed outer shell, then the same atom after both electrons have left, labelled as a magnesium two plus ion.

noteBlocks.md: When a metal reacts it hands over the electrons in its outer shell and becomes a **positive ion**. Magnesium gives away two: $\ce{Mg -> Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$. So the order of the series is simply how willingly each metal does that — **reactivity is the tendency of a metal to form its positive ion**.

noteBlocks.title: Why potassium beats calcium
noteBlocks.md: A potassium atom has one outer electron to give away; a calcium atom has two, and it holds them a little more tightly. Potassium parts with its single electron more easily, so it forms its positive ion more readily and reacts harder with the same water.

noteBlocks.prompt: Reactivity is the tendency of a metal to form its ______ ion.
noteBlocks.explain: Positive. Metals lose electrons, and losing negative charge leaves a positive ion behind.

noteBlocks.md: Heat any of these metals strongly in air and it joins with oxygen to make the **metal oxide**. What tells them apart is what you see while it happens. **Iron** throws **orange sparks**. **Magnesium** burns with a **bright white light** and leaves a white solid. **Copper** never flames: it **glows red**, and a black solid is left. Learn the three sights as well as the products, because the sight is what a question hands you.

noteBlocks.prompt: A metal is heated strongly in air and glows red without sparking. Which metal is it?
noteBlocks.explain: Copper glows red and leaves black copper(II) oxide. Iron sparks orange; magnesium gives the bright white light.

noteBlocks.md:
Only the top three — potassium, sodium and calcium — react with **cold water**, and they give the **metal hydroxide** and **hydrogen**:
calcium + water → calcium hydroxide + hydrogen, or $\ce{Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2}$.
Watch a granule of calcium and there are five things to say: bubbles of gas; the granule sinking and rising as the bubbles lift it; the calcium slowly disappearing; a **colourless** solution with a white solid in it; and the beaker warming up.

noteBlocks.explain: Hydroxide. Cold water always gives the hydroxide; hold on to that, because steam is about to give something different.

noteBlocks.md:
**The question.** Magnesium is heated in a stream of steam. Complete the word equation, and say what the damp mineral wool is for.
**Step 1 — decide which water you are in.** Steam is water in the gas state and it is far hotter, so the products are not the cold-water ones. Magnesium does not react with cold water at all.
**Step 2 — write the products.** Steam gives the metal **oxide** and hydrogen, so: magnesium + steam → magnesium oxide + hydrogen.

noteBlocks.prompt: Finish step 2: zinc + steam → zinc ______ + hydrogen
noteBlocks.explain: Oxide. Every metal that reacts with steam gives its oxide and hydrogen, so zinc behaves exactly as magnesium did.

noteBlocks.md:
**Step 3 — the mineral wool.** It is damp on purpose. Heating it boils the water it is soaked in, and that steam travels down the tube to the magnesium. Its job is to **supply the steam**, not to soak up heat.
**Step 4 — read off the observations.** Inside the tube you would see a bright white light, and a white solid left where the ribbon had been.

noteBlocks.prompt: So what is the damp mineral wool for?
options: heating it boils the water in it, which supplies the steam
it absorbs the heat so the tube does not crack
it dries the hydrogen before it is collected
noteBlocks.answer: heating it boils the water in it, which supplies the steam
noteBlocks.explain: It is the steam generator. Drying the gas is a different job done by a different chemical, and nothing here needs a heat shield.

noteBlocks.md: Every reaction here makes **hydrogen**, and a question will ask how it is collected. It is collected **over water**, because hydrogen is **insoluble**: it bubbles up, pushes the water out of the tube and stays there. To test it, hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube — hydrogen burns with a **squeaky pop**.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why can hydrogen be collected over water?
options: it burns with a squeaky pop
noteBlocks.explain: Because it does not dissolve, it survives the journey up through the water. Being lighter than air is why upward delivery also works, and the pop is the test, not the reason.

steps.working: Steam is hot water vapour, so this is a metal reacting with water — but at steam temperature.
steps.decision: Decide which of the two water reactions you are in before you write anything. Cold water and steam give different products.
Steam gives the metal OXIDE and hydrogen. Magnesium hydroxide belongs to the cold-water reaction, and magnesium does not react with cold water at all.

options: Because steam reactions give the oxide, and cold-water reactions give the hydroxide
Because magnesium is too reactive to make a hydroxide
Because hydroxides only form with Group 1 metals
whyMenu.explain: The split is by the water, not the metal: cold water → hydroxide + hydrogen; steam → oxide + hydrogen.

steps.working: The damp mineral wool is there to make the steam: heating it boils the water it is soaked in.
steps.decision: Say what it produces, not what it absorbs. 'To absorb the heat' and 'to give out heat' were both recorded as wrong in Summer 2025.

steps.working: First observation: a bright white light where the ribbon burns.
steps.decision: An observation is something you can see or feel. Name the light, not the chemistry.

steps.working: Second observation: a white solid is left where the magnesium ribbon was.
steps.decision: Two observations means two different ones. A colour and a state beat two ways of saying the same thing.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) magnesium + steam → magnesium oxide + hydrogen. (b) Heating the damp mineral wool boils the water in it, which supplies the steam. (c) A bright white light, and a white solid left where the ribbon was.

A small piece of sodium is dropped onto cold water in a trough.
(a) Name the two products of the reaction. [2]
(b) Write the balanced symbol equation, including state symbols. [3]
(c) Explain, in terms of electrons, why potassium reacts with cold water more vigorously than sodium. [2]

steps.working: Sodium is one of the top three, so it reacts with COLD water: sodium hydroxide + hydrogen.
steps.decision: Cold water gives the hydroxide. Sodium oxide is the reaction with air, and CCEA lists it as a recurring error.

steps.working: Formulae first: Na, H2O, NaOH, H2.
steps.decision: Write every formula before you balance. Hydrogen is diatomic, so the gas is H2, never H. The formulae are a mark of their own before any balancing is done.

steps.working: Na + H2O → NaOH + H2 has two hydrogens on the left and three on the right, so it is not balanced. Doubling the sodium and the water fixes it: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2.
steps.decision: Balance by changing the numbers in front, never the formulae. Changing H2 to H would be a formula change and scores nothing.

options: Because a balancing number in front is the only thing you are allowed to change
Because H2O can be written as HO if it helps the balance
Because the arrow lets you add an extra hydrogen
whyMenu.explain: A formula is fixed by the chemistry; only the big numbers in front may change. Summer 2024's C2 Foundation report records CaO being rewritten as CaO2 to force a balance.

steps.decision: Sodium is a solid, the water is a liquid, the hydroxide dissolves so it is aqueous, and hydrogen leaves as a gas.

steps.working: A sodium atom and a potassium atom each have one outer electron, but potassium's is further from the nucleus, so potassium loses it more easily and forms its positive ion more readily.
steps.decision: The mark is for the electron, not for the word 'vigorous'. Reactivity is the tendency to form the positive ion.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. (b) 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g). (c) Both atoms have one outer electron, but potassium loses its outer electron more easily, so it forms its positive ion more readily and reacts more vigorously.

items.stem: In a word equation, what goes on the right-hand side of the arrow?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.5 — you are not expected to have met this topic yet

options.feedback: Reactants on the left, products on the right. That is all you need before starting this lesson.
Those are on the left. The arrow means 'turns into', so what comes out is written after it. The lesson below uses word equations from the second section on.
A catalyst is written above the arrow when it is shown at all. The right-hand side is for the products.

items.stem: Which of these is the correct formula for hydrogen gas?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.5 — the diatomic elements

options.feedback: Hydrogen travels as a molecule of two atoms, so every equation in this lesson ends in H₂.
A single H is one atom, not the gas. Hydrogen is diatomic, so the gas is H₂ — worth checking before you start, because every reaction here makes it.
That is water. The gas given off in this topic is hydrogen, H₂.

items.stem: Sodium is in Group 1 of the Periodic Table. How many electrons does a sodium atom have in its outer shell?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.6 — group number and outer electrons

options.feedback: The group number is the number of outer electrons for Groups 1 to 7, and that single electron is why sodium is so reactive.
Two outer electrons would put it in Group 2. Section 1 of the lesson turns this fact into the whole reactivity series, so it is worth fixing first.
Eight is a full outer shell, which is what the Group 0 gases have. Sodium has one.

items.stem: Which of these four metals is the most reactive?
items.skill: Recall the order of the reactivity series

options.feedback: Potassium is at the top of the series: it forms its positive ion most readily of the eight.
Zinc sits below magnesium and aluminium. It reacts with steam, but not with cold water.
Iron is second from the bottom of the eight. Only copper is less reactive.
Copper is the least reactive of the eight: it will not react with water or with steam.

items.stem: Magnesium is heated in a stream of steam. What are the products?
items.skill: Choose the products of a metal with steam

options.feedback: Steam gives the metal oxide and hydrogen.
The hydroxide comes from cold water, and magnesium does not react with cold water. Steam gives the oxide.
Water is a reactant here, not a product. The gas made is hydrogen, which is why it can be collected.
Both halves need changing: the product is the oxide, and the gas is hydrogen, not oxygen.

items.stem: In the magnesium and steam experiment, what is the damp mineral wool for?
items.skill: State the purpose of a piece of apparatus

options.text: heating it boils the water in it, which supplies the steam
options.feedback: That is the whole job: it is the steam generator.

options.text: it absorbs the heat so the tube does not crack
options.feedback: Summer 2025 examiners recorded exactly this answer as a loss. The wool is the source of the steam, not a heat shield.

options.text: it dries the hydrogen before it is collected
options.feedback: The wool is damp on purpose. Drying agents such as anhydrous calcium chloride do the opposite job, and they sit elsewhere.

options.text: it stops the magnesium ribbon sliding down the tube
options.feedback: The wool is at the closed end, away from the ribbon. It is heated to make steam.

items.stem: Which metal does not react with cold water?
items.skill: Separate the cold-water metals from the rest

options.feedback: Iron needs steam. Only potassium, sodium and calcium react with cold water.
Potassium reacts with cold water fiercely, melting and skidding across the surface.
Sodium reacts with cold water, giving sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.
Calcium is the third of the cold-water three, and it is the one CCEA usually puts in a trough.

items.stem: A metal is heated in air and gives off orange sparks. Which metal is it?
items.skill: Match an observation in air to its metal

options.feedback: Iron sparks orange. Fine iron wool is the usual demonstration.
Copper glows red without sparking. Examiners in both 2025 papers recorded iron and copper being swapped here.
Magnesium burns with a bright white light, which is hard to look at directly.
Zinc is not one of the three CCEA names for this table; the sparks belong to iron.

items.stem: Hydrogen from a metal and steam is collected over water. Which property of hydrogen makes that possible?
items.skill: Give the physical property behind a collection method

options.feedback: Insoluble, so it collects instead of dissolving away. That is the one-word answer CCEA prints.

options.text: it is less dense than air
options.feedback: That is why hydrogen can also be collected by upward delivery. Over water, the property that matters is that it does not dissolve.

options.text: it burns with a squeaky pop
options.feedback: That is the test for hydrogen, not a reason for the collection method. The question asks for a physical property.
Hydrogen is far less dense than water; and density is not what decides whether a gas can be collected over it.

parts.stem:
A technician hands you three unlabelled samples of metal. They are calcium, zinc and copper, but you do not know which is which.
Describe how you could use cold water and steam to decide which sample is which, and explain what you would see in each test.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist chemical terms used widely and accurately; organised with clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist chemical vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: add a piece of each metal to cold water and watch for a reaction
only the calcium reacts with cold water, giving bubbles of gas and a colourless solution
calcium + water gives calcium hydroxide and hydrogen
heat the other two in a stream of steam from damp mineral wool
the zinc reacts with steam, giving zinc oxide and hydrogen; the copper does not react at all
the order of reactivity is therefore calcium, then zinc, then copper
reactivity is the tendency of a metal to form its positive ion, so calcium loses its outer electrons most easily

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Two tests, in order: cold water first, then steam on whatever is left.
Every test needs both a method and an observation; a method with no observation is half a point.
Check which water each product came from before you write it: cold water gives calcium hydroxide, steam gives zinc oxide.
parts.workedSolution: Drop a small piece of each metal into cold water. Only one reacts: bubbles of gas rise from it, it slowly disappears and a colourless solution with a white solid in it is left. That sample is the calcium, and the products are calcium hydroxide and hydrogen. Take the other two and heat each in turn in a stream of steam, made by heating damp mineral wool at the closed end of a boiling tube. One of them reacts, glowing and leaving a white solid, and hydrogen is given off, which can be collected over water because it is insoluble. That sample is the zinc, and the products are zinc oxide and hydrogen. The third sample does nothing in cold water or in steam, so it is the copper. The order of reactivity is calcium, then zinc, then copper, because reactivity is the tendency of a metal to form its positive ion and calcium gives up its outer electrons most easily of the three.

findTheMistake.stem:
Órlaith is asked: 'Magnesium is heated in a stream of steam. Complete the word equation and state why the damp mineral wool is there. [3]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Heating the damp mineral wool boils the water in it, which supplies the steam.
The hydrogen is collected over water because it is insoluble.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The gas is right and the collection is right, but the solid product is not. Cold water gives a metal hydroxide; steam gives the metal oxide. Magnesium does not react with cold water at all, so magnesium hydroxide cannot be the product here.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: hydrogen is right and so is the mineral wool. The oxide mark is the one that goes, because the hydroxide belongs to the cold-water reaction and magnesium does not react with cold water at all. Summer 2025 examiners reported this exact swap on the Foundation paper.

prompts.prompt: List the eight metals of the reactivity series in order, most reactive first.
prompts.answer: Potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper.

prompts.prompt: Which metals react with cold water, and what are the two products?
prompts.answer: Potassium, sodium and calcium. They give the metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

prompts.prompt: Which metals react with steam, and what are the two products? Why is the answer not the hydroxide?
prompts.answer: Magnesium, zinc and iron. They give the metal oxide and hydrogen. Steam is hot enough to strip the water right down, so the oxide forms; the hydroxide only comes from cold water.

prompts.prompt: What do you see when iron, magnesium and copper are each heated in air?
prompts.answer: Iron gives orange sparks; magnesium burns with a bright white light; copper glows red. Each leaves the metal oxide behind.

prompts.prompt: In the metal-and-steam experiment, what is the damp mineral wool for, and how is the gas collected?
prompts.answer: Heating the damp mineral wool boils the water in it and supplies the steam. The hydrogen is collected over water, because hydrogen is insoluble in water.

prompts.prompt: Finish the sentence: the reactivity of a metal is its tendency to …
prompts.answer: … form its positive ion, by losing its outer electrons. The more easily a metal loses them, the higher it sits in the series.

prompts.prompt: Complete both: calcium + water → ______ + ______ , and magnesium + steam → ______ + ______ .
prompts.answer: Calcium hydroxide + hydrogen; magnesium oxide + hydrogen.
